title: But They Didn't Recognize Him — Grain, Recognition, Silver
blocks: Peace be with you, brothers and sisters. Today I want to put a very quiet question to you, and it is a question that stings: if a thing has gone twenty-two years without ever once being mentioned, does that mean it is over?
In Genesis chapter 42, ten brothers are shut up for three days. And on the third day they say something to one another — something they had not said once in twenty-two years:
"We are certainly guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us, and we wouldn't listen. Therefore this distress has come upon us." (Genesis 42:21)
So Joseph did beg, down there in the bottom of the pit. So they did hear him. So they chose not to listen.
Chapter 37 never wrote that sentence down. Twenty-two years later, they say it themselves.
1. He Recognized Them; They Did Not Recognize Him
"Now Jacob saw that there was grain in Egypt, and Jacob said to his sons, 'Why do you look at one another?'" (Genesis 42:1)
"Look at one another" is תִּתְרָאוּ (*titra'u*), literally "you keep looking at each other." Ten grown men staring into each other's faces, and not one of them moves.
Why does nobody move? Because moving means going down to Egypt. And Egypt is the one direction on the map that none of them wants to touch.
Jacob says, "Go down there, and buy for us from there, so that we may live, and not die."

But he will not let Benjamin go, "for he said, 'Lest perhaps harm happen to him.'" — and "harm" is אָסוֹן (*ason*), Jacob's private refrain all through this chapter; it comes round twice in the one chapter.

And notice how the text names Benjamin: "Benjamin, Joseph's brother." In Jacob's own heart, ten of them are sons, and that one is "Joseph's brother." Twenty-two years on, the business of that coat is still sitting there.
"Joseph was the governor over the land. It was he who sold to all the people of the land. Joseph's brothers came, and bowed themselves down to him with their faces to the earth." (Genesis 42:6)

"Bowed themselves down" is וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲווּ (*vayishtachavu*). That dream back in chapter 37 — the sheaves standing round about and bowing down to the sheaf in the middle — is fulfilled in this verse, to the letter.
Twenty-two years ago they said, "We will see what will become of his dreams." Now they are seeing it. They simply do not know that they are standing inside the dream.
In verses 7 and 8 there are two words from one and the same root, and they face in exactly opposite directions.
"Joseph saw his brothers, and he recognized them" — "recognized" is וַיַּכִּרֵם (*vayakkirem*).
"But acted like a stranger to them" — the Hebrew is וַיִּתְנַכֵּר (*vayyitnakker*), literally "he made himself foreign."
One word is "to recognize", the other is "to make oneself a stranger", and both are built on the root נָכַר (*nakar*). What Joseph is doing here is hiding himself on purpose.
"Joseph recognized his brothers, but they didn't recognize him." (Genesis 42:8)

Brothers and sisters, that one sentence is worth sitting down with. They cannot recognize him, and half the reason is on the surface: twenty-two years have gone by, his head is shaved, he is dressed as an Egyptian, he is speaking Egyptian, and an interpreter is doing the talking. The other half lies much deeper — in their hearts, that younger brother died a long time ago.

And very often that is exactly why we fail to recognize what God is doing in our own lives. We have already put him in a certain place inside our hearts — and so he can stand right in front of us and we will not know him.
And then Joseph does something a great many readers cannot make sense of: he "spoke roughly with them", and he accuses them of being spies.
"Roughly" is קָשׁוֹת (*qashot*) — simply "hard things", a handful of hard words.
Why does he not make himself known on the spot? He holds absolute authority. He could take his revenge that very hour; he could just as easily throw his arms round them and weep. He does neither.
Because there is one thing he has to know: in these twenty-two years, have they changed?
He holds absolute authority. Why does he not make himself known on the spot, and speak roughly with them instead?

There were in fact two much easier roads open to him: take his revenge at once, or put his arms round them and weep at once. He took neither. Because there was one thing he had to know — in these twenty-two years, have they changed? And in particular: if another one of their father's favourite younger sons were to fall into their hands, would they sell him the same way? Everything arranged over the next few chapters — keeping Simeon back, requiring Benjamin to come, putting the cup into the sack — is set up to ask that one question. And it gives us a distinction well worth holding on to: forgiveness and trust are not the same thing. Forgiveness can be given immediately; trust takes time and evidence. What Joseph does is to forgive first, and then to test, slowly.
"He recognized them, but they didn't recognize him" — why could they not recognize him?

Half the reason is on the outside: twenty-two years have passed, his head is shaved, he wears Egyptian clothes, he speaks Egyptian, an interpreter stands between them. The other half is deeper — in their hearts that brother died long ago. When a person cannot recognize the one standing in front of him, it is usually because he has already assigned him a place inside his own head. And this is well worth taking into our relationship with God. Very often it is the same reason we cannot recognize what God is doing in our lives: we have already decided how he will act and where he will turn up, so he stands right in front of us and we do not know him. To recognize him again, you have to admit that old assumption of yours first.
2. A Light from the Original: Who Is Being Tested?
Three times over Joseph accuses them of being "spies", and it forces them to lay out the family's business one sentence at a time:
"We, your servants, are twelve brothers, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan; and behold, the youngest is today with our father, and one is no more." (Genesis 42:13)
"One is no more" is אֵינֶנּוּ (*einennu*) — "he is not." That is how they have said it for twenty-two years. A sentence half true and half false; say it long enough and you believe it yourself.
And the one who "is no more" is at that very moment sitting in front of them.
Joseph says, "By this you shall be tested." The word is תִּבָּחֵנוּ (*tibbachenu*), and it comes out of the refiner's trade: you put the metal into the fire to find out whether it is the real thing.
He puts them in custody for three days. On the third day he brings them out, and he says something of the first importance:
"Do this, and live, for I fear God." (Genesis 42:18)
The Hebrew word order is emphatic: "That God — he is the one I fear."

Brothers and sisters, that is the greatest authority he holds at this moment, and it is also the deepest restraint upon him. A man with absolute power in his hands, and no God he fears in his heart, will sooner or later do something that runs out of control. Joseph is able to hold back from revenge, and it is not because he has a mild temper. It is because there is Someone above him.

And notice how he goes about it: he offers the way out first and states the condition afterwards — "Do this, and live." He had begun by proposing to keep nine and send one; he changes it to keeping one and sending nine. All the way through, his grip is loosening.
And then, in verse 21, the sentence that has gone twenty-two years without being said comes out:

"They said to one another, 'We are certainly guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us, and we wouldn't listen. Therefore this distress has come upon us.'"
"Certainly" is אֲבָל (*aval*), a word that hardly ever appears in the Old Testament; and when it does appear it means "there is no getting out of this" — the point where a man stops arguing.
"Guilty" is אֲשֵׁמִים (*ashemim*), and it does not mean "we did something wrong"; it means "we are men who owe a debt."
"The distress of his soul" is צָרַת נַפְשׁוֹ (*tzarat nafsho*), and the root of it means "narrow" — his soul was being squeezed.
"When he begged us" — בְּהִתְחַנְנוֹ (*behitchaneno*). Chapter 37 did not write one word of it. Twenty-two years later, they supply the missing picture themselves.

Brothers and sisters, this is what pushing a thing down actually means: a conscience can be held under, and once it is held under a man can go on living an ordinary life for twenty-two years. Marry a wife, father children, pasture the flocks, sit down to eat, laugh. And the whole time, the picture is still there.
It does not disappear because a long time has gone by. It only sinks to the bottom. And the moment pressure comes, the whole of it floats back up — with every detail perfectly clear.
And then verse 24: "He turned himself away from them, and wept."
This is the first time Joseph weeps in Genesis. Before the book is finished he will weep seven times.
Why is he weeping? Because what he had been waiting for was never an apology. What he had been waiting for was this — that at last they were facing themselves.

And just before he weeps, the text goes out of its way to tell us one thing: "They didn't know that Joseph understood them; for there was an interpreter between them." The word for "interpreter" is הַמֵּלִיץ (*hammelits*), and the same word is used in Job chapter 33 for a mediator.
He had understood all along. Every sentence they said, he understood. And he chose to go out and weep first, and to come back and speak afterwards.
"For I fear God" — how much weight is that sentence carrying here?

The Hebrew word order is emphatic: "That God — he is the one I fear." And notice where the man who says it is standing at that moment: he holds absolute authority, and he may do whatever he likes with these ten men in front of him. And he puts himself under a God he fears. A man with absolute power in his hands, and no God he fears in his heart, will sooner or later do something that runs out of control. Joseph is able to hold back from revenge, and it is not because he has a mild temper; it is because there is Someone above him. And to every person who holds any authority at all — parents, managers, leaders — it says exactly the same thing: is there Someone above you?
The sentence that went twenty-two years unsaid — why does it come out only now?

"We are certainly guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us, and we wouldn't listen." That word "certainly" is a Hebrew word that hardly ever appears, and when it does it means "there is no getting out of this"; and "guilty" does not mean "we did something wrong", it means "we are men who owe a debt." And chapter 37 did not write one word about Joseph begging down in that pit — twenty-two years later, it is they themselves who supply the picture. This is what pushing a thing down actually means: a conscience can be held under, and once it is held under a man can go on living an ordinary life for twenty-two years; but the picture is there the whole time, and the moment pressure comes the whole of it floats back up, with every detail perfectly clear.
What Joseph gives next is a single order, and there are three intentions hidden inside it:
"Then Joseph gave a command to fill their bags with grain, and to restore each man's money into his sack, and to give them food for the way." (Genesis 42:25)
First, the bags are filled with grain — they are to live.
Second, the silver goes back — this trip will cost them nothing.
Third, "food for the way" — that item hangs on no condition at all. It is simply given.

Brothers and sisters, the man who was sold for twenty pieces of silver has just sent the silver back. The word behind "money" in this verse is כֶּסֶף (*kesef*), silver — the same word as those twenty pieces. Twenty-two years ago they traded a brother away for silver; now that brother will not take their silver.
But their reaction is a remarkable thing. One of them opens his sack at the lodging place, sees the silver lying there in the mouth of the sack, and says to his brothers, "My money is restored!"
"Their hearts failed them, and they turned trembling to one another, saying, 'What is this that God has done to us?'" (Genesis 42:28)
"Their hearts failed them" is וַיֵּצֵא לִבָּם (*vayyetze libbam*), literally "their heart went out of them" — frightened clean out of their skins.
The very same act of grace, falling onto a heart that owes something, turns into fear.

And that is an entirely real thing. When a person has sin in his heart that has never been dealt with, even good news will frighten him. He dares not take what is given free, because he knows he does not deserve it.
So the order of the gospel is always this: first let a person see his own sin, and then let him understand that the gift costs him nothing. Skip the first step, and grace turns into anxiety.

And there is something else. Joseph had in fact said a comforting thing to them: "you shall trade in the land" (42:34). He was reaching for a long relationship with them. But it never went in. Their heads were full of nothing but that bag of silver.
The silver has been given back to them. Why are they frightened instead?

"Their heart went out of them" — that is what the Hebrew says, word for word: frightened clean out of their skins. The very same act of grace, falling onto a heart that owes something, turns into fear. And that is an entirely real thing: when a person has sin in his heart that has never been dealt with, even good news will frighten him; he dares not take what is given free, because he knows he does not deserve it. So the order of the gospel is always this: first let a person see his own sin, and then let him understand that the gift costs him nothing. Skip the first step, and grace turns into anxiety. And here is the saddest part of it — Joseph had actually said to them, "you shall trade in the land", and it never went in. Their heads were full of nothing but that bag of silver.
Sending the silver back — how does that answer to what happened twenty-two years ago?

Twenty-two years ago they traded a brother away for twenty pieces of silver; now that brother will not take their silver. And Joseph's order has three intentions hidden inside it: the bags filled with grain — they are to live; the silver put back — this trip will cost them nothing; "food for the way" — an item hanging on no condition at all, simply given. Put those three together and you have the very shape of grace: enough to live on, no account kept, and something extra thrown in. And there is a very practical lesson in it for us: real forgiveness is not refusing to mention the thing; it is refusing to go on charging the other person for it. Only when the ledger inside a man has been settled will he ever be capable of throwing in something extra.
4. All These Things Are Against Me
In the last stretch of the chapter the camera goes back to that old father in Canaan.

The sons tell him everything, point by point. And then, as they are emptying out the grain — "behold, each man's bundle of money was in his sack. When they and their father saw their bundles of money, they were afraid." The word for "emptied" is a participle in the Hebrew, an action still going on — and the camera freezes right here.
And then Jacob says the heaviest sentence he speaks in the whole chapter:
"You have bereaved me of my children! Joseph is no more, Simeon is no more, and you want to take Benjamin away. All these things are against me." (Genesis 42:36)
Count the "me" in that sentence: bereaved *me*, *my* children, against *me*.
Simeon is still in an Egyptian prison, the whole household is going hungry, his grandchildren are close to having nothing to eat — and what this father says is: all these things are against me.
Brothers and sisters, this is the sequel to that line back in chapter 34, "You have troubled me." Twenty-two years have gone by, and this father's first thought is still himself.
That is the self-centred life: whatever happens, my first thought is always "what does this do to me?"
And notice: "Joseph is no more, Simeon is no more" — he sets the two of them side by side in one breath; and yet the ten sons standing right in front of him seem hardly to count as sons at all.
Then Reuben speaks up: "Kill my two sons, if I don't bring him to you."
That is a dreadful offer. He puts up his own two sons as security — which is exactly what his father does: solving his own difficulty with somebody else's life.
And back in the earlier scene, at the moment when the brothers were confessing together, what Reuben said was: "Didn't I tell you, saying, 'Don't sin against the child,' and you wouldn't listen?"

Brothers and sisters, when everyone is owning the wrong together, the single most out-of-place sentence anybody can say is "I told you so." That sentence is not help. That sentence is getting yourself off the hook.
Jacob's last word is this: "My son shall not go down with you … then you will bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to Sheol."
And so the chapter ends inside one father's self-pity.

And in the next chapter, Judah — who has been standing there all this while saying nothing — will step out and say, "I'll be collateral for him … then let me bear the blame forever." We read chapter 38 a little while back: the man who learned how to say "I was wrong" is the man who, this time, puts himself up as the pledge.
Jacob says, "All these things are against me." What exactly is wrong with that?

Count the "me" in the sentence: bereaved *me*, *my* children, against *me*. Simeon is still in an Egyptian prison, the whole household is going hungry, his grandchildren are close to having nothing to eat — and what this father says is that all these things are against him. It is the sequel to that line in chapter 34, "You have troubled me" — twenty-two years on, and the first thought is still himself. That is the self-centred life: whatever happens, my first thought is always "what does this do to me?" It can be said in a very wounded tone, with very good reasons behind it, and it can even be made to sound quite spiritual. The way to tell is simple enough: count how many times "me" comes up in the sentence.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
There are several places in this chapter that are very easy to preach backwards.

The first distortion is preaching Joseph's testing of his brothers as calculated revenge. From beginning to end he does them no harm at all: the bags are filled, the silver is put back, the food for the road is given free, and when they confess he turns aside and weeps. What he wants to see is whether they have changed. Preach it as revenge and the congregation will never learn that forgiveness and discernment can live together in the same person. The test is this: when the congregation has heard you, what have they seen — hatred, or waiting?

The second distortion is preaching "forgiveness" as though nothing ever needs checking. Forgiveness is not the same thing as refusing to discern. Joseph builds a whole series of situations precisely in order to see clearly. Get this backwards and the congregation will take indulgence for love, and take "I forgive you" to mean "we shall pretend it never happened."

The third distortion is holding up Reuben's "I told you so" as a good example. At the very moment his brothers are confessing together, he is busy getting himself off the hook. Make that a model, and your congregation will learn to protect themselves first whenever something goes wrong on a team.

The fourth distortion is preaching the brothers' sin and never touching Jacob's self-centred life. That line in verse 36, "All these things are against me", is the long-standing root of this family's disease. Pass over it, and the parents and the elders in the room will never be brought into the light.

The fifth distortion is preaching "Therefore this distress has come upon us" as a formula of cause and retribution — whoever is suffering now must be someone who did something bad before. That is the theology of Job's three friends. What the text records is their own reading of their own situation; it is not the narrator's verdict.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: our families are extremely good at not mentioning things. Something happens; everybody understands without a word being said; the New Year comes round and we still sit down together round the same pot, still put food into one another's bowls, and for twenty years nobody says it. We assume that means it is over. This chapter tells us otherwise: a thing that has never been dealt with does not go away. It only sinks to the bottom. And it will come back up at the least suitable moment of all — usually when there is trouble in the family, when somebody falls ill, when the property has to be divided. Brothers and sisters, this week, take one thing that has been pressed down inside you and say it out, first of all before God. You do not have to go to the person first. Say it through completely in prayer: what happened that day, what I did, and what I knew at the time. A thing has to be sayable before it can be dealt with.

The second question: our elders are very used to governing the whole household by means of their own suffering. "You are all trying to make me die of anger." "I gave my whole life for you." "Here I am, the grey head burying the black head." What Jacob says in this chapter is exactly that kind of speech. Those sentences are not necessarily untrue — but their function is to hold people down. If you are the elder, be careful: your suffering is real, and your suffering ought never to become a chain on your children. If you are the younger, understand this too: you are not responsible for the whole of an elder's emotional life; you are responsible for rendering the honour and the love that are properly yours to render. And this week, if you catch yourself using "look how pitiful I am" to make other people do as you say, please stop.
7. Living 321 Out — Healing First, Then Entrusting
Brothers and sisters, let us bring this lesson back to the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. Joseph turned himself away, wept, and then came back and got on with the business in hand. When the Lord Jesus looked at Jerusalem, he wept over it too; that city was going to crucify him, and it was that city he wept for. My role model is this: when he had authority in his hands, there was no hatred in his heart.

The Bible is my standard. The standard is not "they wronged me, so I have the right to deal with them as I please." The standard is "Repay no one evil for evil", and it is also "There is no fear in love." And the same standard says, "be wise as serpents and harmless as doves" — so checking a thing out is not a failure of trust; it is being responsible.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. When to uncover a thing and when to wait — there is no formula for that. Joseph waited two whole chapters before he made himself known. Rely on your intellect and go it alone, and you will be troubled — you will calculate, you will jump the gun, you will not be able to hold yourself back. Rely on the heart and lean on the Holy Spirit, and you will have joy — he knows the day that person is ready.

Let Jesus be King. He recognized them, and they did not recognize him. He could have taken his revenge on the spot; he could have made himself known on the spot; he did neither. To let Jesus be King means that even the question of when to uncover the thing is handed over to him to settle.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. What he said to them was, "I fear God." He did not say, "I am the governor of this land." What he said was, in effect, "There is Someone above me." Authority is only safe in the hands of a man who gives the glory to God.

Establish God's system. God took twenty-two years, and in them he did not merely prepare a governor; he healed a heart. Put authority into the hands of a man who has never been healed, and that authority will wound people. To establish God's system, the order is this: healing first, and entrusting afterwards.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One and the Same Sack
We come to this chapter carrying four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "I told you so." Reuben said that sentence, and not one person in the room was any better for it. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights — climbing up into the judge's seat. Humility is returning to our originally intended position as a man among men, and saying it alongside your brothers: "We are certainly guilty concerning our brother" — and the word there is "we".

The fearful heart says, "How did the silver get into my sack?" A thing given free frightened them clean out of their skins. To fear, every act of grace looks like a trap. Brothers and sisters, if you find yourself permanently uneasy about God's kindness towards you, that is very unlikely to be discernment. It is far more likely to be a debt you have never settled.

The ashamed heart says, "That is the one thing I will never dare speak of as long as I live." They did not speak of it for twenty-two years either. But the day it came out was not the day they were finished; it was the day the restoring began — and on that day, the man they had wronged was on the other side of the door, weeping.

The wounded heart says, "Isn't an apology what I have been waiting for?" What Joseph was waiting for was not an apology. He was waiting for them to be willing, at last, to face themselves. Sometimes we hold on with both hands to "he has got to say sorry to me", when what we actually want is to know that he understands what he did. That is a thing we cannot extract from anybody. We can only hand it over to God.
Four kinds of heart, and one and the same sack. Inside it there is grain, there is the silver that was put back, and there is a portion of food for the road that nobody ever asked for.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, towards God. Take one thing you have never once admitted, and say it out completely in prayer. The time, the place, what I did, and what I knew at the time. When you have said it, stop there and let him deal with it.
Second, towards yourself. Examine your first thought when bad news arrives. If that thought is always "what does this do to me?", write it down and bring it to the Lord.
Third, towards people. Take the sentence "I told you so" out of your mouth for one week. Especially when somebody else has just failed.
Fourth, towards daily living. This week, do not use busyness to cover over something you know needs dealing with. Write it on a piece of paper, and set a date for it.
Fifth, towards your calling. Pray for one person who is carrying something heavy, and be with him once this week. You do not have to deliver any great truths. Just be there.

Sixth, tell it in three sentences to one friend outside the church. First: there are ten men in the Bible who held one thing down for twenty-two years. Second: the moment pressure came, they poured out every detail themselves — they even remembered how their younger brother had looked while he was begging. Third: so what I have learned is that time does not deal with anything; only facing it does.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that the thing which has sunk to the bottom, I will bring up and say out loud before God.
I declare that I will no longer say "I told you so"; I will carry it together with my brothers.
I declare that my first thought when bad news comes will no longer be myself.
I declare that if there is any authority in my hands, I will remember that there is Someone above me; I fear God.
Why does "I told you so" wound people so badly?

At the moment when everyone was confessing together, Reuben said, "Didn't I tell you, saying, 'Don't sin against the child,' and you wouldn't listen?" In the instant a group of people finally faces itself, that sentence is not help; it is getting yourself off the hook — it lifts the speaker out of the "we" and stands him off to one side as a spectator. In practice there are three things you can say instead: "I had a part in this too; I did not hold my ground at the time"; "What can we do now?"; or nothing at all — listen right through first. And if you really did give the warning early, the worth of that warning lies in whether you are willing to help clear up the mess now, not in who said it first.
On the day the dream came true, the man who dreamed it hid himself and wept.

He had waited twenty-two years, and what came at the end of the waiting was not the thrill of victory but a fit of weeping. Because what he wanted was never that they should kneel. It was that they should come back.

So the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on other people, not on our circumstances. Not I, but Christ. Because we have such a One as well. He recognizes us, and we very often do not recognize him. He holds absolute authority in his hands, and there is no hatred in his heart. He fills the bags with grain, he puts the silver back, and on top of it he gives the food for the road. And on the day we are finally willing to say that sentence — "I am certainly guilty" — there is One on the other side of the door who has already wept for us first.

May God bless every one of us with the courage to say out loud the thing that has sunk to the bottom; may our homes stop being held together by not mentioning things; and may every scrap of authority in our hands be used inside a heart that fears God. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head; the second carries it from the head into the heart; the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — a lesson that never reaches the third transformation has stopped at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if there is time to spare. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be completed at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ A conscience can be held under, and a man can still live twenty-two perfectly ordinary years on top of it. What does that say to the idea that time washes everything away?
2. ★★ Forgiveness can be given immediately; trust takes time and evidence. How do you tell whether you are testing someone or taking revenge on him?
3. ★ The same act of grace, falling onto a heart that owes something, turns into fear. Why can the order of the gospel never be reversed?
4. ★★ "All these things are against me" — how many times does "me" come up in that one sentence? What does the self-centred life actually look like?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I told you so), fearful (I am afraid that thing will be dug up again), ashamed (I heard someone begging and I did not move), wounded (nobody has ever asked me how I am). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read "for I fear God" aloud, and then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there something inside you that you have held down for many years? What is it that keeps it there to this day?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The debt I owe is …" (You may say no more than "I know what mine is.")
9. ★★ This week, who are you going to say "I had a part in this too" to? Say the name and say when.

Leader's reminder: this section will turn up old matters going back many years. Anyone at all may answer with nothing more than "I know what mine is." Do not press for details, do not call in each other's debts, and follow up with people privately after the meeting; where a matter involves the law or would injure another person, help them seek pastoral and professional advice.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own family, is there an account you are still collecting on? Say how you intend to settle it.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or in your service, what is the sentence you most often reach for to get yourself off the hook?

12. ★★★ The practice of not saying "I told you so": this week, swap that sentence for "I had a part in this too" or "What can we do now?" Name the situation in which it is most likely to slip out of your mouth.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and ask him to pull you up this week the moment you say "I told you so." Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there are ten brothers in the Bible who sold their younger brother, and for twenty-two years nobody mentioned it. Second: twenty-two years later, when trouble came, the first thing out of their mouths was "We are certainly guilty concerning our brother" — and they remembered, perfectly clearly, the picture of their brother begging down in the pit. Third: so what I have learned is that time does not wear away a thing that has never been dealt with. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the matter you have held down for many years (you may say no more than "I know what mine is"), and the "I had a part in this too" that you are going to say this week. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord for the courage to face ourselves, and for the freedom to settle that account.
